contract_plain_english: For every real random variable X, if X is sub-gaussian according to the source’s Section 2.5 definition, then X is sub-exponential according to its Section 2.7 definition. This body sentence asserts no converse and no quantitative comparison of the two norms.

source_evidence.anchor: Section 2.7 body paragraph immediately before Lemma 2.7.6
source_evidence.observation: The source says literally: ‘First, any sub-gaussian distribution is clearly sub-exponential. (Why?)’ It states a one-way class inclusion and gives no quantitative norm bound in this sentence.
The source calls X sub-gaussian when it satisfies one of properties i–iv of Proposition 2.5.2 and defines ∥X∥ψ2 = inf {t > 0 : E exp(X²/t²) ≤ 2}.

Proposition 2.7.1 gives equivalent exponential-tail, linear-moment-growth, exponential-moment, and bounded-exponential-moment properties. Definition 2.7.5 calls X sub-exponential when it satisfies one of properties a–d and displays ∥X∥ψ1 = inf {t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) ≤ 2}.

binders: A real-valued random variable X (the body sentence phrases the claim in terms of its distribution).
conclusions: X is sub-exponential in the sense of Definition 2.7.5 / Proposition 2.7.1.
definitions_and_conventions: Sub-gaussian and sub-exponential mean satisfaction of the respective equivalent property families identified by Definitions 2.5.6 and 2.7.5.
hypotheses: X is sub-gaussian in the sense of Definition 2.5.6 / Proposition 2.5.2.
implicit_context: The claim appears in Section 2.7 after the two property characterizations and before the square and product lemmas.
The same ambient probability law is used for all probabilities and expectations concerning X.

details: The source asserts sub-gaussian ⇒ sub-exponential only; it does not assert the converse.
The claim applies to any sub-gaussian distribution.
No centering, independence, boundedness, or nondegeneracy assumption is stated.
The body sentence states class membership only and does not state a ψ1-versus-ψ2 constant.

undebatable_constraints: The implication must run from sub-gaussian to sub-exponential.
The conclusion is class membership, with no quantitative norm inequality supplied by this source sentence.
No mean-zero or independence hypothesis may be added.
The sub-gaussian and sub-exponential notions must be the source notions tied to Definitions 2.5.6 and 2.7.5.
